{{Short description|Prime number of the form that allows fast modular reduction}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Solinas prime,''' or '''generalized Mersenne prime''', is a [[prime number]] that has the form <math>f(2^m)</math>, where <math>f(x)</math> is a low-[[degree of a polynomial|degree]] [[polynomial]] with small [[integer]] [[coefficient]]s.<ref>{{cite tech report |first=Jerome A. |last=Solinas |title=Generalized Mersenne Numbers |number=CORR-99-39 |institution=Center for Applied Cryptographic Research, University of Waterloo |year=1999 |url=http://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/techreports/1999/corr99-39.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Encyclopedia of Cryptography and Security|url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediacryp00tilb_374|url-access=limited|first=Jerome A.|last=Solinas|editor-first1=Henk C. A. van|editor-last1=Tilborg|editor-first2=Sushil|editor-last2=Jajodia|date=2011|publisher=Springer US|pages=[https://archive.org/details/encyclopediacryp00tilb_374/page/n549 509]–510|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-5906-5_32|chapter = Generalized Mersenne Prime|isbn = 978-1-4419-5905-8}}</ref> These primes allow fast modular reduction algorithms and are widely used in [[cryptography]]. They are named after Jerome Solinas.

This class of numbers encompasses a few other categories of prime numbers:
* [[Mersenne primes]], which have the form <math>2^k-1</math>,
* Crandall or pseudo-Mersenne primes, which have the form <math>2^k-c</math> for small [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] <math>c</math>,<ref>{{cite patent |country=US |number=5159632 |status=patent |title=Method and apparatus for public key exchange in a cryptographic system |gdate=1992-10-27 |fdate=1991-09-17 |pridate= |invent1=Richard E. Crandall |assign1=NeXT Computer, Inc. |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5159632A/en }}</ref> including <math>c=</math> 3 {{OEIS|A050414}}, 5 {{OEIS|A059608}}, 7 {{OEIS|A059609}}, 9 {{OEIS|A059610}}, etc.

==Modular reduction algorithm==
Let <math>f(t) = t^d - c_{d-1}t^{d-1} - ... - c_0</math> be a [[monic polynomial]] of degree <math>d</math> with coefficients in <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> and suppose that <math>p = f(2^m)</math> is a Solinas prime. Given a number <math>n < p^2</math> with up to <math>2md</math> bits, we want to find a number [[modular arithmetic|congruent]] to <math>n</math> mod <math>p</math> with only as many bits as <math>p</math> – that is, with at most <math>md</math> bits.

First, represent <math>n</math> in base <math>2^m</math>:

:<math>n = \sum_{j=0}^{2d-1}A_j2^{mj}</math>

Next, generate a <math>d</math>-by-<math>d</math> [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] <math>X = (X_{i,j})</math> by stepping <math>d</math> times the [[linear-feedback shift register]] defined over <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> by the polynomial <math>f</math>: starting with the <math>d</math>-integer register <math>[0 | 0 |...| 0 | 1]</math>, shift right one position, injecting <math>0</math> on the left and adding (component-wise) the output value times the vector <math>[c_0,...,c_{d-1}]</math> at each step (see [1] for details). Let <math>X_{i,j}</math> be the integer in the <math>j</math>th register on the <math>i</math>th step and note that the first row of <math>X</math> is given by <math>(X_{0,j}) = [c_0,...,c_{d-1}]</math>. Then if we denote by <math>B = (B_i)</math> the integer vector given by:

:<math>(B_0 ... B_{d-1}) = (A_0 ... A_{d-1}) + (A_d ... A_{2d-1})X</math>,

it can be easily checked that:

:<math>\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}B_j2^{mj}\equiv\sum_{j=0}^{2d-1}A_j2^{mj} \mod p</math>.

Thus <math>B</math> represents an <math>md</math>-bit integer congruent to <math>n</math>.

For judicious choices of <math>f</math> (again, see [1]), this algorithm involves only a relatively small number of additions and subtractions (and no divisions!), so it can be much more efficient than the naive modular reduction algorithm (<math>n - p \cdot (n / p)</math>).

==Examples==
In 1999, [[NIST]] recommended four Solinas primes as moduli for [[elliptic curve cryptography]]:<ref>{{cite tech report |title=Recommended Elliptic Curves for Federal Government Use |institution=[[NIST]] |year=1999 |url=https://csrc.nist.rip/groups/ST/toolkit/documents/dss/NISTReCur.pdf }}</ref>
* curve p-192 uses modulus <math>2^{192} - 2^{64} - 1</math>
* curve p-224 uses modulus <math>2^{224} - 2^{96} + 1</math>
* curve p-256 uses modulus <math>2^{256} - 2^{224} + 2^{192} + 2^{96} -1</math>
* curve p-384 uses modulus <math>2^{384} - 2^{128} - 2^{96} + 2^{32} - 1</math>.

A newer [[Curve448]] uses modulus <math>2^{448} - 2^{224} - 1</math>.

A Solinas prime that fits into a typical 64-bit unsigned integer is <math>2^{64}-2^{32}+1</math>, it is <math>\Phi_{192}(2)</math> where <math>\Phi</math> is the [[cyclotomic polynomial]], thus it is a [[unique prime]] in [[binary numeral system|base 2]] (with [[period length]] 192). This size is too small for cryptography, but finds use in implementing a [[number-theoretic transform]] for efficient multiplication of large numbers.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Craig-Wood |first1=Nick |title=Integer DWTs mod 2^64-2^32+1 |url=https://www.craig-wood.com/nick/armprime/math/ |website=www.craig-wood.com}}</ref>

A complete list of <math>f(2^k)=2^m - 2^n \pm 1</math> with <math>m \leq 2000</math>, a small modular reduction weight <math>wt < 15</math>, and <math>k=8,16,32,64</math> (i.e. multiples of a [[computer word]] size) was produced by José de Jesús Angel Angel and Guillermo Morales-Luna in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |last1=de Jesús Angel Angel |first1=José |last2=Morales-Luna |first2=Guillermo |title=Solinas primes of small weight for fixed sizes |url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/058 |website=Cryptology ePrint Archive, Paper 2010/058 |date=2010}}</ref>

The [[Curve25519]] uses <math>2^{255} - 19</math>, which has also been called pseudo-Mersenne.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Nath |first1=Kaushik |title=Efficient Arithmetic In (Pseudo-)Mersenne Prime Order Fields |date=2018 |url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/985 |access-date=2025-05-10 |id=2018/985 |last2=Sarkar |first2=Palash}}</ref>
